questions.question: How do you write a unit test for a Spring @Service using Mockito?
questions.title: Unit Test Spring Service Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to run the test with Mockito, @Mock to create a mock repository, and @InjectMocks to inject that mock into your service. This is a true unit test—no Spring context loads, runs in milliseconds. Only use @SpringBootTest when you need the full application context for integration testing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between a fast unit test and a Spring integration test, and can avoid loading the full context unnecessarily
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @SpringBootTest to every service test, which loads the entire Spring context and makes the test suite 50-100x slower
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete unit test with proper assertions and explain that avoiding Spring context startup is the key to a fast test suite

sections.title: Unit Testing Spring Services with Mockito
sections.content:
Unit testing a Spring service means testing the service's business logic in isolation—without loading the entire Spring application context. **Mockito** lets you create mock objects for dependencies like repositories or external APIs, and **MockitoExtension** runs JUnit 5 tests with Mockito support.

The key annotations are **@Mock** (creates a mock dependency), **@InjectMocks** (injects mocks into the service under test), and **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** (activates Mockito in JUnit 5). This approach is fast—tests run in 10-50 milliseconds because there's no Spring container startup.

Think of it like testing a single gear in a machine: you control what comes in from connected parts (the mocks) and verify what comes out (the result). This is the foundation of test-driven development in Spring Boot—write hundreds of these fast unit tests to cover business logic, then add a handful of slower integration tests to verify the layers work together.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pure Unit Test|~No Spring context|the ExtendWith MockitoExtension|Mock the deps|InjectMocks the service
blue|The Flow|~Arrange, act, assert|stub the repository|call the service method|assert and verify
emerald|Why No Context|~Speed and focus|milliseconds not seconds|tests logic only|context means integration

sections.title: Complete Unit Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use Mockito-based unit tests for **all business logic in your service layer**—calculations, validations, decision trees, data transformations. If your OrderService has a method that calculates discounts based on customer tier and order amount, write a unit test that mocks the repository and verifies the discount logic.

Use this when you want **fast feedback**—running 500 unit tests should take under 10 seconds.

Use it when testing **edge cases and error paths**: mock the repository to throw an exception, then verify your service handles it correctly. Don't use this approach for testing repository query logic (use @DataJpaTest) or controller request/response handling (use @WebMvcTest)—those need the actual Spring layers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding @SpringBootTest to service tests**: Freshers often add @SpringBootTest because it's familiar from tutorials, but this loads the entire application context—database connections, web server, all beans—making each test take 2-5 seconds instead of 10 milliseconds. A 100-test suite goes from 1 second to 5 minutes.
- **Not verifying mock interactions**: Writing when(...).thenReturn(...) but never calling verify() means you don't check if your service actually called the repository. Your test passes even if the service never saves the order.
- **Mocking the class under test**: Using @Mock on OrderService and @InjectMocks on the same class—Mockito can't inject a mock into itself. The service under test should be @InjectMocks, its dependencies should be @Mock.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Activates Mockito in JUnit 5 tests, enabling @Mock and @InjectMocks annotations
- **@Mock**: Creates a mock object for a dependency—all methods return null/0/false unless you stub them with when()
- **@InjectMocks**: Creates the real service instance and injects all @Mock dependencies into it automatically
- **when().thenReturn()**: Stubs a mock method—defines what the mock should return when called with specific arguments
- **verify()**: Asserts that a mock method was called with expected arguments—crucial for testing side effects
- **No Spring context**: Pure Mockito tests run without Spring, so they start instantly and execute in single-digit milliseconds
- **Use for business logic**: Perfect for testing calculations, validations, orchestration—anything that doesn't need database or HTTP

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To write a unit test for a Spring service using Mockito, you start by annotating the test class with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class. That's the JUnit 5 way to activate Mockito. Then you create mocks for the service's dependencies using at-Mock. For example, if your OrderService depends on an OrderRepository, you'd write at-Mock private OrderRepository orderRepository. Next, you annotate the service itself with at-InjectMocks, which tells Mockito to create a real OrderService instance and inject the mock repository into it. Inside your test method, you use when and thenReturn to define the mock's behavior. Say when orderRepository dot save is called with any Order, return a saved Order with an ID. Then you call your service method and use JUnit assertions to verify the result. The key thing here is this runs without Spring—no application context, no database connection, nothing. It's pure Java object testing. That's why it's so fast. You can run hundreds of these tests in a couple seconds. One mistake I see freshers make is adding at-SpringBootTest to these tests. That loads the entire Spring application, which takes several seconds per test. For unit testing service logic, you don't need Spring at all. Save at-SpringBootTest for end-to-end integration tests where you're testing the whole application flow.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and slice test annotations?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Spring Boot | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest loads the entire application context—all beans, all auto-configuration, full Spring Boot environment. Slice tests like @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest load only the relevant layer (web, JPA, JSON serialization). Slice tests are faster and more focused; use @SpringBootTest only for true end-to-end integration tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot's layered testing strategy and when to use each approach for speed and focus
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test because it's the most familiar annotation, leading to slow test suites
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the common slice tests, explain what each loads, and describe a concrete scenario where @SpringBootTest is the right choice

sections.title: Full Context vs Layered Testing Strategy
sections.content:
Spring Boot offers two testing philosophies: **@SpringBootTest** loads the complete application—every bean, every auto-configuration, database connections, web server, the works. It recreates your production environment in test mode. **Slice tests** like @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest load only one layer of your application. @WebMvcTest loads controllers and Spring MVC, @DataJpaTest loads repositories and JPA.

The trade-off is speed versus scope. @SpringBootTest takes 3-8 seconds to start because it initializes the entire Spring container. Slice tests take 200-800 milliseconds because they load only what's needed for that layer. Think of @SpringBootTest like testing a car by driving it on a road—you verify everything works together but setup is slow. Slice tests are like testing individual components on a workbench—the engine, the brakes, the electrical system—each test is fast and focused. In a well-structured Spring Boot project, you have hundreds of slice tests (fast feedback on individual layers) and maybe 10-20 @SpringBootTest integration tests (verify the layers integrate correctly).

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|SpringBootTest|~Full context|every bean loaded|slow and broad|end-to-end
blue|Slice Tests|~Partial context|WebMvcTest, DataJpaTest|fast and focused|just one layer
emerald|Pick Rule|~Slice by default|SpringBootTest sparingly|unit test most logic|a pyramid shape

sections.title: Code Example
SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @SpringBootTest | Slice Tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Beans Loaded | All application beans and auto-config | Only beans for target layer |
| Startup Time | 3-8 seconds full context | 200-800ms layer-specific context |
| Database | Connects to configured database | @DataJpaTest uses embedded H2 |
| Web Server | Starts embedded Tomcat by default | @WebMvcTest runs MockMvc in-memory |
| Use Case | End-to-end integration tests | Fast focused layer tests |

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **@SpringBootTest** for end-to-end integration tests that verify multiple layers working together—a REST endpoint calls a service that calls a repository that hits the database. For example, testing that POST /api/orders with a JSON body successfully saves to the database and returns 201 Created.

Use it when you need to test **cross-cutting concerns** like security filters, transaction propagation across layers, or message queue integration.

Use **@WebMvcTest** for testing REST controllers—request handling, parameter binding, response formatting, error handling.

Use **@DataJpaTest** for repository query logic—custom JPQL, derived finders, entity relationships.

Use **@JsonTest** for testing Jackson serialization and deserialization of DTOs.

Use **plain Mockito tests** (no Spring) for service business logic. The rule: start with the fastest test that gives you confidence, escalate to slower tests only when necessary.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for all tests**: Freshers learn @SpringBootTest first and use it everywhere because it "just works". But a 200-test suite where every test loads the full Spring context takes 10-15 minutes to run. Developers stop running tests frequently, bugs slip through. The right mix is 80% slice tests and Mockito, 15% @SpringBootTest integration tests, 5% end-to-end tests.
- **Misunderstanding slice test scope**: Adding @DataJpaTest to a controller test or @WebMvcTest to a repository test fails because the needed beans aren't loaded. Each slice test annotation loads specific Spring Boot auto-configuration slices.
- **Not mocking external dependencies in @SpringBootTest**: Running @SpringBootTest against real external APIs or message queues makes tests flaky and slow. Use @MockBean to replace those beans with mocks even in full-context tests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@SpringBootTest**: Loads the complete Spring application context—use for end-to-end integration tests, not unit tests
- **Slice tests**: Category of annotations (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest) that load only one application layer
- **Speed difference**: @SpringBootTest takes 3-8 seconds to start, slice tests take 200-800ms—matters when you have hundreds of tests
- **@WebMvcTest**: Loads web layer (controllers, filters, advice), auto-configures MockMvc, requires @MockBean for services
- **@DataJpaTest**: Loads JPA layer (repositories, entities), auto-configures embedded H2, wraps tests in rollback transactions
- **Test pyramid**: Majority of tests should be fast slice tests and Mockito unit tests, minority should be @SpringBootTest
- **@MockBean**: Spring's mock annotation that adds a Mockito mock to the application context—works in any Spring test

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference between at-SpringBootTest and slice test annotations is scope and speed. at-SpringBootTest loads your entire Spring Boot application—every bean, every auto-configuration, database connections, the embedded web server if you have one. It recreates your production environment in test mode. That's powerful for integration tests where you want to verify the whole application works end-to-end, but it's slow. Starting the full Spring context takes three to eight seconds. Now slice tests like at-WebMvcTest, at-DataJpaTest, at-JsonTest load only the specific layer you're testing. at-WebMvcTest loads just the web layer—controllers, filters, controller advice—and configures MockMvc so you can test HTTP requests. at-DataJpaTest loads just the JPA layer—repositories and entities—and starts an embedded H2 database. Because they load less, they start much faster, usually under a second. The right testing strategy is to use slice tests and plain Mockito for the majority of your tests. Like 80 percent. They give you fast feedback. Then use at-SpringBootTest for maybe 15 to 20 percent of your tests—the critical end-to-end flows where you want to verify multiple layers integrate correctly. A common mistake freshers make is using at-SpringBootTest for everything because it's the first annotation they learn. But when you have 200 tests and each one loads the full Spring context, your test suite takes 15 minutes to run. Developers stop running tests. That's when bugs slip in.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring REST controller using MockMvc?
questions.title: Spring MockMvc Controller Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @WebMvcTest on your test class to load only the Spring MVC layer—controllers, filters, advice. Inject MockMvc to perform HTTP requests in memory. Mock the controller's service dependencies with @MockBean. Use mockMvc.perform() to send requests and andExpect() to assert on status codes, headers, and JSON response body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring MVC layer testing—a core skill for Spring Boot REST API development
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest and TestRestTemplate when @WebMvcTest with MockMvc is faster and more focused on the controller layer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete test with JSON path assertions and explain that @WebMvcTest only loads web layer beans, not services or repositories

sections.title: Testing REST Controllers with MockMvc
sections.content:
Testing a Spring REST controller means verifying it correctly handles HTTP requests and returns the right responses—status codes, headers, JSON body. **@WebMvcTest** is a Spring Boot slice test annotation that loads only the web layer: your controllers, any @ControllerAdvice, filters, and Spring MVC configuration. It doesn't load services or repositories, so you mock those with **@MockBean**. **MockMvc** is the test object you inject to perform HTTP requests in memory—no actual web server starts.

You call mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/1")) to simulate a GET request, then chain .andExpect(status().isOk()) and .andExpect(jsonPath("$.item").value("Laptop")) to assert the response. Think of MockMvc like a flight simulator: it recreates the full HTTP request-response cycle—URL routing, parameter binding, JSON serialization—without leaving the JVM. This lets you test all your controller logic: path variables, request bodies, error handling, validation failures, 404 vs 200 responses. These tests run in 50-200 milliseconds because they skip service and database layers.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|MockMvc|~Test controllers|no real server|the WebMvcTest slice|the fast HTTP layer
blue|The Flow|~Simulate a request|perform get or post|andExpect a status|assert the JSON
emerald|Mock the Service|~the MockBean annotation|controller in isolation|stub service calls|verify the mapping

sections.title: Complete Controller Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content: Use @WebMvcTest with MockMvc for **testing all your REST controller endpoints**—GET, POST, PUT, DELETE. Test that path variables bind correctly: does /orders/123 actually pass 123 to your service? Test request body deserialization: if a client sends invalid JSON or missing required fields, does your controller return 400 Bad Request? Test your **@ExceptionHandler and @ControllerAdvice** classes: when the service throws OrderNotFoundException, does the controller return 404 with the right error message? Use this to verify **security annotations**: does @PreAuthorize block unauthorized users? Don't use this for testing service business logic (use plain Mockito) or database queries (use @DataJpaTest). This is purely for the HTTP layer—URL routing, parameter extraction, response formatting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest with TestRestTemplate**: Freshers often write controller tests with @SpringBootTest and make real HTTP calls via TestRestTemplate. This starts the entire application including the embedded Tomcat server, making tests 10x slower. @WebMvcTest is faster because it only loads the web layer and runs requests in-process.
- **Forgetting @MockBean for services**: If you use @WebMvcTest without mocking the controller's service dependency, Spring can't find a bean for OrderService and the test fails with a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. You must add @MockBean for every service the controller uses.
- **Not testing error responses**: Writing tests only for the happy path—order found, user created—but never testing 404 Not Found, 400 Bad Request, or 500 Internal Server Error scenarios. Production controllers spend half their time handling errors.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@WebMvcTest**: Spring Boot slice test that loads only the web layer—controllers, filters, advice—skipping services and repositories
- **MockMvc**: Injected test object that performs HTTP requests in memory—no real web server starts, tests run in-process
- **@MockBean**: Spring's version of @Mock that creates a mock bean and adds it to the test application context
- **mockMvc.perform()**: Starts an HTTP request—use get(), post(), put(), delete() with the endpoint path
- **andExpect()**: Chains assertions on the response—status(), jsonPath(), header(), content() matchers available
- **jsonPath()**: JSONPath expression syntax for asserting on nested JSON fields—dollar sign dot field accesses the root object
- **Focused testing**: Tests only the controller layer—request handling, response formatting, error handling—services are mocked

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test a Spring REST controller using MockMvc, you start by annotating the test class with at-WebMvcTest and passing your controller class. For example, at-WebMvcTest OrderController dot class. This tells Spring Boot to load only the web layer—your controller, any filters, controller advice, but not services or repositories. Then you inject MockMvc using at-Autowired. MockMvc is the tool you use to perform HTTP requests. Next, you mock the controller's service dependencies with at-MockBean. So if OrderController depends on OrderService, you'd write at-MockBean private OrderService orderService. In your test method, you stub the service behavior with when and thenReturn, just like regular Mockito. Then you call mockMvc dot perform with the HTTP method and endpoint—like get slash API slash orders slash 1. You chain andExpect calls to assert the response: andExpect status is OK, andExpect jsonPath dollar dot item dot value Laptop. JSONPath is like XPath for JSON—dollar is the root, dot accesses fields. The huge advantage here is you're testing the full HTTP cycle—URL routing, parameter binding, JSON serialization—without starting a web server. These tests run in under 200 milliseconds. A common mistake freshers make is using at-SpringBootTest with TestRestTemplate instead. That actually starts an embedded Tomcat server and makes real HTTP calls, which is much slower and overkill for testing a single controller.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.title: Spring Data JPA Repository Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @DataJpaTest to load only the JPA layer with an embedded H2 database. This slice test auto-configures Spring Data JPA repositories, runs each test in a transaction that rolls back after the test completes. Test custom @Query methods, derived query methods, and entity constraints here—no mocking needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JPA repository testing with a real database slice, not mocked repositories
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to test repository query logic by mocking the repository itself, which defeats the purpose—you can't test SQL/JPQL queries against a mock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @DataJpaTest uses an in-memory database and transaction rollback, so tests don't pollute each other and run fast

sections.title: Testing JPA Repositories with Real Database
sections.content:
Testing a Spring Data JPA repository means verifying your custom queries, derived finder methods, and entity relationships work correctly against a real database. **@DataJpaTest** is a Spring Boot slice test annotation that loads only the persistence layer: JPA repositories, entity classes, and an **embedded H2 database**. No web controllers, no services—just the data access layer. Each test method runs inside a transaction that **automatically rolls back** when the test completes, so data changes don't leak between tests. You inject your repository with @Autowired and call its methods directly—no mocking. If you have a custom @Query that finds orders by customer email, you save test data, call the method, and assert the results.

Think of this as testing your database queries in a sandbox: H2 is an in-memory SQL database that behaves like PostgreSQL or MySQL but exists only while the test runs. This approach catches real-world issues: typos in JPQL queries, incorrect join conditions, missing indexes on query columns. These tests run in 100-500 milliseconds because H2 is pure Java, no network, no disk I/O.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the DataJpaTest slice|~Repository layer only|in-memory or Testcontainers|rolls back per test|fast
blue|What to Test|~Custom queries|derived methods|JPQL correctness|not Spring's plumbing
emerald|Gotcha|~Don't mock the repo|use a real DB slice|test the actual SQL|trust generated CRUD

sections.title: Complete Repository Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use @DataJpaTest for **testing custom @Query methods**—complex JPQL or native SQL queries that join multiple tables or use aggregate functions. If you write a query that finds the top 10 customers by total order value in the last 30 days, write a @DataJpaTest that inserts test customers and orders, runs the query, and verifies the results.

Use it for **testing derived query methods**: Spring Data generates SQL from method names like findByCustomerEmailAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc, but does it work correctly? Test it.

Use it for **testing entity constraints and relationships**: does your @ManyToOne cascade delete correctly? Does @Column(unique=true) actually enforce uniqueness? Don't use this for testing service layer business logic—that should be a pure Mockito unit test with a mocked repository.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking the repository in these tests**: Freshers sometimes add @Mock for the repository even in @DataJpaTest, which completely defeats the purpose. You're testing the repository's actual query logic against a database—mocking it means you're not testing anything real.
- **Not using TestEntityManager to set up data**: Calling repository.save() in test setup works, but TestEntityManager gives you more control—persistAndFlush() ensures data hits the database immediately, and you can clear the persistence context to test lazy loading behavior.
- **Forgetting transaction rollback is automatic**: Manually calling entityManager.clear() or repository.deleteAll() after each test is unnecessary noise—@DataJpaTest wraps each test in a transaction that rolls back. Your test data never leaks to the next test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@DataJpaTest**: Spring Boot slice test that loads only JPA repositories, entities, and an embedded H2 database
- **Embedded H2**: In-memory SQL database that mimics production databases but runs entirely in the JVM—no external setup needed
- **Automatic rollback**: Each test runs in a transaction that rolls back after completion—tests don't pollute each other's data
- **TestEntityManager**: Test-specific EntityManager that provides explicit control over persistence context—use persistAndFlush() and flush()
- **Test real queries**: You're testing actual SQL execution against a database—catches JPQL syntax errors, join mistakes, constraint violations
- **No mocking**: You inject the real repository and call its methods directly—this is an integration test at the persistence layer
- **Fast enough**: Despite using a real database, tests run in 100-500ms because H2 is in-memory with no network latency

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test a Spring Data JPA repository, you use at-DataJpaTest annotation on the test class. This is a slice test, meaning it loads only the persistence layer—your repositories, entity classes, and it automatically configures an embedded H2 database. H2 is an in-memory SQL database written in Java, so it starts instantly and runs entirely in the JVM. No Docker, no external database needed. You inject your repository with at-Autowired, just like in production code. The key difference from other tests is you're not mocking the repository here. You're testing its actual query logic against a real database. So if you have a custom at-Query method that finds orders by customer email, you'd use TestEntityManager to insert a test customer and orders, then call your repository method and assert it returns the right results. One crucial thing: each test runs in a transaction that automatically rolls back when the test finishes. That means data you insert in one test doesn't affect the next test. You don't need to manually clean up. This is perfect for testing derived query methods—those Spring Data methods where you write findByCustomerEmailAndStatus and Spring generates the SQL. You want to make sure that generated SQL actually works. A mistake I see is freshers trying to mock the repository in these tests. That defeats the whole point. You can't test a SQL query against a mock. The mock just returns whatever you tell it to. Use at-DataJpaTest when you want to verify your database queries are correct.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @MockBean in Spring Boot tests?
questions.title: @Mock vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @Mock is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a mock object with no Spring involvement—used in plain unit tests. @MockBean creates a mock and registers it as a Spring bean in the application context, replacing the real bean—used in Spring Boot tests like @WebMvcTest or @SpringBootTest.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when to use each annotation and the performance cost of loading a Spring context just for mocking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in a plain unit test that doesn't load Spring, which doesn't work and shows confusion about what each annotation does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean forces Spring to rebuild the application context if the mock set changes, making tests slower, so use @Mock whenever you don't need Spring

sections.title: Two Ways to Mock in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
When testing Spring Boot applications, you have two ways to create mock objects. **@Mock** is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a lightweight mock object completely outside the Spring framework—it's what you use in fast unit tests where you manually inject dependencies into your service. **@MockBean** is a Spring Boot annotation that creates a mock AND registers it as a bean in the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of that type—it's what you use when you need Spring to auto-wire the mock into other beans during integration tests.

The key difference is **context loading**: @Mock has zero Spring overhead (tests run in milliseconds), while @MockBean forces Spring to start up and manage the application context (tests run in seconds). Use @Mock by default for pure unit tests; only reach for @MockBean when you're testing Spring-managed components like controllers or need Spring's dependency injection to wire the mock into multiple layers.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~Plain Mockito|no context|fast unit tests|the ExtendWith extension
blue|the MockBean annotation|~Spring context|swaps a real bean|integration or slice|slower
emerald|Pick Rule|~Mock for pure logic|MockBean with SpringBootTest|or slice tests|don't mix carelessly

sections.title: Code Example
@Mock vs @MockBean Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Mock | @MockBean |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Framework | Pure Mockito, no Spring | Spring Boot specific |
| Context Loading | No Spring context needed | Loads/rebuilds application context |
| Test Speed | Milliseconds (instant) | Seconds (context startup overhead) |
| Dependency Injection | Manual constructor injection | Spring auto-wires into beans |
| Test Annotation | @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) | @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest |

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: **Use @Mock** when you're writing fast unit tests for a single class in isolation—testing OrderService business logic by mocking OrderRepository. You instantiate the service yourself, pass the mock via constructor, and run the test without Spring. Your test class uses @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and nothing else. **Use @MockBean** when you need Spring's integration features—testing a REST controller with @WebMvcTest and mocking the service layer so MockMvc can auto-wire everything, or testing a scheduled job with @SpringBootTest where the job needs access to multiple Spring-managed beans. The rule of thumb: if you're calling new YourService(mockRepo) in the test, use @Mock. If Spring is creating the service instance for you, use @MockBean.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @MockBean without a Spring test annotation**: Freshers annotate a test with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and use @MockBean, then wonder why the mock is null—@MockBean only works when Spring is managing the test class, requiring @SpringBootTest or similar.
- **Overusing @MockBean in unit tests**: Developers use @MockBean everywhere because it seems more powerful, causing every test to load the full Spring context and run 100x slower—a test suite that should take 5 seconds takes 8 minutes.
- **Not realizing context caching breaks**: Each unique set of @MockBean annotations creates a new application context, so mocking different beans in different test classes defeats Spring's context caching and multiplies test time.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Mock**: Mockito annotation for lightweight mocks in pure unit tests with no Spring context
- **@MockBean**: Spring Boot annotation that creates a mock and registers it as a Spring bean in the context
- **Performance**: @Mock tests run in milliseconds; @MockBean tests run in seconds due to context startup
- **Context rebuilding**: Every unique combination of @MockBean mocks forces Spring to create a new context
- **Manual vs auto-wiring**: @Mock requires constructor injection in test; @MockBean uses Spring's dependency injection
- **Test annotations**: @Mock works with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class); @MockBean requires @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest
- **Default choice**: Prefer @Mock for speed; use @MockBean only when you need Spring's integration features

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is that at-Mock is pure Mockito and at-MockBean is Spring Boot specific. When you use at-Mock, you're creating a lightweight mock object that has nothing to do with Spring. You manually inject it into your class under test using the constructor. The test runs super fast because no Spring context loads—we're talking milliseconds. This is what you use for true unit tests where you're testing one service class in isolation. On the other hand, at-MockBean creates a mock and registers it as a bean in the Spring application context. Spring then auto-wires this mock into any other beans that need it. You'd use this in integration tests with at-WebMvcTest or at-SpringBootTest where you need Spring to manage the wiring. The tradeoff is that at-MockBean tests are much slower because they have to start up the Spring context, which can take several seconds. One thing that catches freshers off guard is that at-MockBean also forces Spring to rebuild the application context if you change which beans you're mocking across different test classes. This breaks context caching and can make your test suite really slow. So the rule I follow is: use at-Mock by default for fast unit tests, and only reach for at-MockBean when you actually need Spring's dependency injection to wire things together.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service that has a @Transactional method?
questions.title: Testing a @Transactional Spring Service
questions.direct_answer: For unit tests, mock the repository and test business logic without transactions—@Transactional has no effect without a Spring context. For integration tests, use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to load the transaction infrastructure, then verify transaction behavior like rollback on exceptions or cascade operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that @Transactional is a Spring proxy behavior that only works when Spring's context is active, not in plain unit tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to test transaction rollback in a unit test where no Spring context is loaded, expecting @Transactional to work without the transaction proxy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that unit tests focus on business logic and integration tests verify transaction behavior, and that @Transactional requires Spring's AOP proxy to function

sections.title: Testing Transactional Services at Two Levels
sections.content:
Testing a **@Transactional** service requires understanding that the annotation is not Java language behavior—it's a **Spring AOP proxy** that wraps your method in transaction management code. This means there are two distinct testing approaches. **Unit tests** focus on the business logic inside the method: mock the repository, stub its methods, and verify your service's logic works correctly—the @Transactional annotation is ignored because no Spring context exists to create the proxy. **Integration tests** focus on the transactional behavior itself: use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to load Spring's transaction infrastructure, then verify that transactions commit when methods succeed, roll back when exceptions are thrown, or propagate across multiple repository calls. The common mistake is trying to verify rollback behavior in a unit test—without Spring's transaction proxy active, @Transactional is just a decoration with no runtime effect.

Think of it this way: unit tests verify "what the method does", integration tests verify "how Spring wraps the method in transaction boundaries".

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Unit Test Reality|~No real transaction|Transactional is a proxy|inactive without context|tests logic only
blue|What to Verify|~Behaviour, not rollback|stub the repo|assert the results|verify the save calls
emerald|Rollback Testing|~Needs a context|SpringBootTest|a real or H2 database|integration territory

sections.title: Unit Test Example for Transactional Service
When to Use Each Testing Approach
sections.content: **Use unit tests** (with mocked repositories) when you want to verify the service's business logic, decision-making, and interactions with dependencies—checking that it calls the right repository methods in the right order, handles validation correctly, or throws the right exceptions. These tests are fast and focus on the code you wrote, not Spring's infrastructure. **Use integration tests** (with @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest) when you need to verify transactional behavior that only exists at runtime—confirming that multiple repository saves happen in a single transaction, that a RuntimeException triggers a rollback so no data is saved to the database, or that cascade deletes work correctly across entity relationships. Integration tests are slower but catch issues where your transaction boundaries are misconfigured or where lazy-loading triggers unexpected database queries.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting @Transactional to work in unit tests**: Freshers write a unit test with MockitoExtension, mock the repository, then try to verify rollback behavior—but @Transactional needs Spring's AOP proxy to function, which doesn't exist in a plain unit test, so nothing happens.
- **Testing only the happy path**: Developers verify that the service saves data when everything works but never test what happens when a repository throws an exception—missing the chance to verify that @Transactional correctly rolls back partial changes.
- **Loading full @SpringBootTest for simple logic tests**: Using @SpringBootTest to test basic validation logic that doesn't need database access or transactions, making tests 10x slower than a simple unit test with mocks would be.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **@Transactional is a Spring proxy**: The annotation only works when Spring's AOP infrastructure is active, not in plain unit tests
- **Unit test focus**: Mock repositories and test business logic, decision flow, and method interactions—@Transactional is ignored
- **Integration test focus**: Load Spring context with @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to verify transaction commit, rollback, and propagation
- **Rollback verification**: Use integration tests to confirm that exceptions trigger rollback and no data persists to the database
- **Test pyramid principle**: Write more unit tests for business logic (fast, isolated) and fewer integration tests for transaction behavior (slower, comprehensive)
- **No transaction in mocked context**: When you mock a repository, no real database exists, so transaction semantics cannot be tested
- **AOP proxy requirement**: Spring must create a proxy around your service for @Transactional to intercept method calls and manage transactions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Testing a Transactional service depends on what you want to verify. For unit tests, you ignore the at-Transactional annotation completely. You mock the repository using at-Mock, stub its methods with Mockito, and test your business logic—like does the service validate the order correctly, does it call save in the right sequence. The at-Transactional annotation doesn't do anything in this context because there's no Spring context to create the transaction proxy. It's just a decoration on the method. For integration tests, you actually need Spring to be running. You'd use at-DataJpaTest if you're testing repository interactions, or at-SpringBootTest if you need the full application context. This loads Spring's transaction infrastructure, so now at-Transactional actually works. You can verify things like: if the method throws an exception, does the transaction roll back so no data is saved to the database. Or if you save multiple entities, do they all commit together in one transaction. The key thing freshers miss is that at-Transactional is a Spring AOP proxy feature—it wraps your method at runtime with transaction management code. Without Spring running, that proxy doesn't exist, so the annotation has no effect. So my approach is: unit tests for business logic with mocks, integration tests for transaction behavior with a real database.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service method that calls an external REST API?
questions.title: Testing Services with External REST Calls
questions.direct_answer: Mock the RestTemplate or WebClient dependency with @Mock, use when().thenReturn() to stub its HTTP methods—exchange, getForObject, etc.—with a test response, then assert that your service processes that response correctly. This keeps tests fast and doesn't depend on external APIs being available.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to isolate external HTTP dependencies in unit tests so tests are fast, deterministic, and don't require network access
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting the test make actual HTTP calls to external APIs, making tests slow, flaky, and dependent on external service availability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WireMock or MockWebServer for integration-level HTTP testing where you need more realistic request/response matching than Mockito provides

sections.title: Isolating External REST API Calls in Tests
sections.content:
When a Spring service calls an external REST API using **RestTemplate** or **WebClient**, you want your tests to be **fast, deterministic, and isolated**—not dependent on the external API being online, responding quickly, or returning consistent data. The solution is to **mock the HTTP client** itself.

In unit tests, you inject a mocked RestTemplate or WebClient into your service using **@Mock**, then stub its methods like **getForObject()**, **exchange()**, or **retrieve()** to return canned responses. Your test then verifies that your service correctly processes that response—parses JSON, handles errors, transforms data. This approach keeps tests running in milliseconds with no network calls. For more realistic testing where you need to match request URLs, headers, or bodies—like verifying your service sends the right Authorization header—you'd use **WireMock** or **MockWebServer** to spin up a fake HTTP server that responds to real HTTP requests. But for most unit testing, Mockito stubbing is enough and much simpler.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Mock the Client|~No real network|stub RestTemplate or WebClient|deterministic responses|fast tests
blue|Test Scenarios|~Cover all paths|a success response|an error status|a timeout or exception
emerald|Verify|~The right call made|the correct URL and args|an argument captor|retry behaviour

sections.title: Mocking RestTemplate in Service Test
When to Use Each Testing Approach
sections.content: **Use Mockito mocks** (stubbing RestTemplate or WebClient) for fast unit tests where you're testing your service's logic—how it transforms the API response, handles null fields, or throws exceptions on error status codes. These tests run instantly and don't require starting any servers. You're verifying "given this HTTP response, does my service do the right thing". **Use WireMock or MockWebServer** for integration-level tests where you need to verify the actual HTTP request your service sends—correct URL path, query parameters, headers like Authorization or Content-Type, request body formatting. These tools start a real HTTP server on localhost, your service makes real HTTP calls to it, and you assert on the received requests. This catches issues like wrong URL construction, missing headers, or incorrect JSON serialization that Mockito stubbing wouldn't detect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Making real HTTP calls in tests**: Freshers don't mock the HTTP client at all, so tests actually call the external API—this makes tests slow (network latency), flaky (API might be down or rate-limited), and dependent on external service availability.
- **Not testing error responses**: Developers only stub the success case where the API returns 200 OK, but never test what happens when the API returns 500, 404, or throws a timeout exception—leaving error handling code untested.
- **Mocking the service instead of the client**: Beginners mock the entire service layer instead of just the RestTemplate, which defeats the purpose—you want to test that your service correctly uses the HTTP client, so you mock the client, not the service itself.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Mock the HTTP client**: Use @Mock on RestTemplate or WebClient, not on your service—you're testing the service logic
- **Stub HTTP methods**: Use when().thenReturn() to stub getForObject, postForObject, exchange, or retrieve with test responses
- **No network calls**: Mocking the client means tests run instantly with no actual HTTP requests sent over the network
- **Test error cases**: Stub the client to throw RestClientException or return error status codes to verify your service's error handling
- **WireMock for integration**: Use WireMock or MockWebServer when you need to verify actual HTTP request details like headers or URL parameters
- **Constructor injection**: Inject RestTemplate via constructor so you can easily swap in a mock during testing
- **Verify interactions**: Use verify() to assert that your service called the HTTP client with the expected URL and request body

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When your service calls an external REST API, you definitely don't want your tests making real HTTP calls. That would make them slow, flaky, and dependent on the external service being up. Instead, you mock the RestTemplate or WebClient dependency. In the test, you use at-Mock to create a mock HTTP client, then inject it into your service via the constructor. Then you stub the HTTP method using Mockito's when-thenReturn. For example, if your service calls restTemplate.getForObject to fetch user data, you'd stub that method to return a fake user object. Now when your service runs in the test, it gets that canned response instead of making a real network call. You then assert that your service processes that response correctly—maybe it extracts a field, transforms the data, or caches it. One thing to watch for is testing error cases too. You should stub the RestTemplate to throw a RestClientException or return an error response, then verify your service handles it gracefully—logs the error, returns a default value, or throws a custom exception. For more advanced scenarios where you need to verify the actual HTTP request details—like does my service send the right authorization header—you'd use WireMock. That starts a fake HTTP server on localhost and lets you assert on the incoming requests. But for most unit tests, mocking RestTemplate with Mockito is simpler and faster.

questions.question: How do you test exception handling in a Spring @Service — for example, when a repository throws a DataAccessException?
questions.title: Testing Exception Handling in Spring Services
questions.direct_answer: Stub the mock to throw the exception using when().thenThrow(), then use assertThrows() from JUnit 5 to verify that your service throws the expected exception or handles it correctly. Test both propagation—service re-throws the exception—and translation—service wraps the exception in a domain-specific exception.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to write negative-path tests that cover error handling code, ensuring your service behaves correctly when dependencies fail
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only testing the happy path and leaving exception handling branches untested, resulting in low code coverage and unverified error logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the case where the service propagates the exception unchanged and the case where it translates/wraps it into a custom domain exception with context

sections.title: Testing the Unhappy Path with Exceptions
sections.content:
Exception handling is where many production bugs hide—code that only runs when dependencies fail. To test it, you **stub your mocked dependency to throw an exception** using Mockito's **when().thenThrow()**, then verify your service responds correctly.

There are two common patterns: **propagation** where your service re-throws the exception unchanged (letting it bubble up to the controller or caller), and **translation** where your service catches the exception and wraps it in a **custom domain exception** with additional context. For example, when the repository throws **DataAccessException**, your service might catch it and throw **OrderNotFoundException** with the order ID and a user-friendly message. You verify this with **assertThrows()** from JUnit 5, which captures the thrown exception so you can assert on its type, message, and cause. Testing exceptions ensures your error handling code is correct and gives you confidence that your service fails gracefully when the database is down or returns unexpected errors.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Stub the Failure|~Force an error|then throw on the mock|simulate a downstream fail|trigger the catch
blue|Assert the Outcome|~assertThrows|check the exception type|verify the message|wrapped or rethrown
emerald|Verify Side Effects|~What happens on error|no commit|the error is logged|a fallback is called

sections.title: Testing Exception Handling in Service
When to Test Each Exception Pattern
sections.content: **Test propagation** when your service is a thin wrapper around a repository and you want infrastructure exceptions to bubble up unchanged—like a simple CRUD service where DataAccessException is meaningful to the caller and will be handled by a global exception handler in the controller layer. Verify that the service doesn't accidentally swallow or change the exception. **Test translation** when your service adds business logic and the low-level exception isn't meaningful to callers—like catching EmptyResultDataAccessException and throwing OrderNotFoundException with the specific order ID that failed. This gives better error messages and hides infrastructure details from the API layer. You should test both the exception type and the message content, and verify that the original exception is preserved as the cause for debugging.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only testing the happy path**: Freshers write tests where everything succeeds—repository returns data, external API responds—but never test what happens when dependencies throw exceptions, leaving error handling code with zero test coverage.
- **Using try-catch in tests**: Developers write try-catch blocks in test methods to capture exceptions, making tests verbose and easy to get wrong—JUnit 5's assertThrows is cleaner and returns the exception for further assertions.
- **Not verifying the exception message or cause**: Tests assert that the right exception type is thrown but don't check the message or wrapped cause, missing bugs where error context is lost or the wrong exception is wrapped.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **when().thenThrow()**: Stub mocked dependencies to throw exceptions simulating failure scenarios like database errors or timeouts
- **assertThrows()**: JUnit 5 method that verifies an exception is thrown and returns it for additional assertions on message or cause
- **Propagation pattern**: Service re-throws the exception unchanged—test that the original exception escapes unmodified
- **Translation pattern**: Service catches low-level exception and throws a domain-specific exception with context—test message and cause
- **Test negative paths**: Exception handling is where bugs hide—always test error cases, not just success scenarios
- **Verify exception details**: Assert on exception type, message content, and that the original exception is wrapped as the cause
- **Coverage metric**: Untested catch blocks tank code coverage and represent real production risk when dependencies fail

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To test exception handling in a service, you stub the mock dependency to throw an exception using when-thenThrow. For example, if you're testing a service that calls a repository, you'd mock the repository and make findById throw a DataAccessException to simulate a database failure. Then you use assertThrows from JUnit 5 to verify your service handles it correctly. assertThrows takes the expected exception class and a lambda that calls your service method. If that exception is thrown, the test passes and assertThrows returns the exception so you can make additional assertions on it. There are two patterns you typically test. The first is propagation, where your service just lets the exception bubble up unchanged. You'd verify that the same exception type escapes the service. The second is translation, where your service catches the low-level exception and wraps it in a custom domain exception with more context. For example, catching DataAccessException and throwing OrderNotFoundException with the specific order ID that failed. In that case, you'd assert on the custom exception type, check that the message includes the order ID, and verify that the original exception is preserved as the cause using getCause. The common mistake freshers make is only testing the happy path—when everything works—and leaving all the catch blocks untested. That tanks your code coverage and means your error handling code has never actually run until it fails in production.
